title: Halteverbotszone Berlin - Quick Summary
items: **The kerb outside your door is not yours on moving day.** You need a temporary no-stopping order, a **Halteverbotszone**, from the traffic authority of the district that kerb sits in. Berlin calls the service **Haltverbot für Umzüge** and the fee starts at **21 euros**.

**The order does not come with signs.** No Berlin office hands them over. You rent the physical signs from a private firm, which in Berlin starts at roughly **45 to 50 euros** for a simple one-address package, and you are responsible for putting them up and taking them down.

**Count back thirty-two days, not fourteen.** Berlin publishes an average processing time of **about four weeks**, and the signs have to be standing **four days** before the van arrives. Applying two weeks ahead, which most removal guides suggest, is already late.

**Three full days is the number that decides the towing bill.** The Bundesverwaltungsgericht set that lead time in May 2018. If the signs went up later, a car that was already parked there can still be moved, but its driver does not have to pay for it. The court counts whole calendar days and makes no exception for weekends.

**Most moves need two zones and two offices.** One kerb at the old address, one at the new, and the two addresses are often in different districts. The email addresses follow no pattern: Mitte answers on sga@, Neukölln on svb@, Friedrichshain-Kreuzberg on tiefgruen@.

**Two districts hide their desk.** Charlottenburg-Wilmersdorf and Steglitz-Zehlendorf are the only ones where Berlin's service page sends you to the borough homepage instead of a contact, so the planner on this page carries the addresses I dug out for all twelve, checked on **16 September 2026**.
